sentences.text: Polaris is the star many people call the North Star.
It is famous, but it is not the brightest star in the night sky.
Earth spins around an imaginary line called its axis.
That axis points almost straight at Polaris, so Polaris seems to stay still.
Other stars look as if they slowly circle around it during the night.
If you can find Polaris, you are looking about north.
Travelers have used that sky clue for a very long time.
The star is not useful in the same way from the southern half of Earth, because it sits in the northern sky.
A compass can also show north, but Polaris is a star, not a magnet.
To find it, some people start with the Big Dipper.
They follow the two stars on the outer edge of the Dipper's cup.
Those pointer stars lead the eye toward Polaris.
Knowing one steady star can keep a traveler from walking in circles.

questions.prompt: What is this passage mostly about?

choices.text: Why Polaris helps people find north
How to build a brighter star
Why the Big Dipper is a planet
How magnets are melted into stars

questions.explanation: The passage explains that Polaris seems still because of Earth's axis, and that finding it means you are looking about north. That use is the main idea.

questions.prompt: Is Polaris the brightest star in the night sky?

choices.text: Yes. It is the brightest star of all.
No. It is famous, but not the brightest.
Yes, but only in the daytime.
No, because it is really a planet.

questions.explanation: The passage says Polaris is famous, but it is not the brightest star in the night sky. That detail surprises many readers on purpose.

questions.prompt: In this passage, Earth's axis is what?

choices.text: The brightest star in the Dipper
The imaginary line Earth spins around
The path of a river at night

questions.explanation: The passage defines axis as the imaginary line Earth spins around. That line points almost at Polaris.

questions.prompt: A traveler watches one very bright star for an hour and sees it change position. What can the traveler figure out?

choices.text: The star must be Polaris, because bright stars never move
The traveler is looking at a compass needle
Earth has stopped spinning for the night
That star is probably not Polaris, because Polaris seems to stay still

questions.explanation: The passage says Polaris seems to stay still while other stars seem to circle. A bright star that changes position does not match the clue for Polaris.
